D012-D018_h001.question:
It started after that crash landing two years ago. We hit severe turbulence on approach, lost an engine, and for a few minutes I was sure we were all going to die. Nobody did, but a lot of passengers were badly hurt. I still see the blood in the cabin when I close my eyes.

Since then, anything medical sets me off. If I have to get blood drawn, or my wife turns on a hospital show, my heart takes off, my hands shake, I start sweating, and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. I sometimes have to leave the room during the preflight safety briefing videos if they show injuries.

But it’s not just that. I’m having nightmares about the incident several times a week—waking up drenched, hearing the alarms in my head. I get flashbacks in the cockpit if we hit turbulence; for a moment I’m back in that descent. I avoid talking about that flight, avoid flying over that same route if I can. I’m always on edge, jumpy at sudden noises, and I can’t seem to relax, even at home. This has been going on pretty much continuously since the accident.
D012-D018_h001.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D012-D018_h002.question:
I plan a lot of outdoor weddings, so I’m used to scouting venues, driving over bridges, using service elevators, that kind of thing. About eight months ago, I was driving home from a reception and a truck slammed into my car on a narrow bridge. My car spun and almost went over the edge. Since then, my whole relationship with bridges and tunnels has changed.

Now, if I even see that bridge on the GPS, my chest tightens, my heart starts pounding, and I’ll reroute 30 minutes out of the way to avoid it. If I get stuck in traffic on a bridge or in a tunnel, it’s like I’m back in the crash: I start sweating, shaking, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something terrible is about to happen. It kicks in immediately, before I even have time to think it through.

It’s not just the fear, though. I keep having flashes of the accident—at night, in the shower, even during ceremonies. I jolt awake from nightmares about falling off bridges. I’m jumpy with loud noises, exhausted from poor sleep, and I avoid any venue that requires crossing a bridge, which is starting to affect my work and my marriage.
D012-D018_h002.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D012-D018_h003.question:
It started about a year ago, after that robbery at my shop. The man had a gun in my face, screaming; ever since then, loud, sudden noises set me off. If someone drops a tray in the store or a car backfires outside, my whole body goes rigid. I can’t move, can’t speak, I just freeze there like I’m back behind the counter with him yelling. My heart pounds, my hands go numb, and all I can think is, “He’s here again.”

It’s not only fear of the noise itself; it’s like my brain replays the whole thing. I see his jacket, smell his cologne, hear the shouting. At night I wake up from dreams where I’m being robbed again, sometimes even shot. I avoid busy markets and crowded malls because they’re too loud, and I’m constantly checking the door and the security cameras in my shop.

Even at home with my husband, I’m jumpy, on edge. I don’t feel like myself anymore—tired, irritable, and always half-expecting something terrible to happen the moment there’s any sudden sound.
D012-D018_h003.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D012-D018_h004.question:
It started after that car accident about a year ago. I was driving home from a late census run, and a truck slammed into the side of our car on the bridge. I thought I was going to die. Ever since then, I can’t stand bridges or tunnels. Even seeing one on my route map makes my heart pound. If I have to cross a bridge for work, I start shaking, sweating, and I feel like I can’t breathe the second I see the entrance. I’ll sometimes pull over and cry rather than go across.

But it isn’t just the driving. I keep reliving the accident. I get these flashbacks when I’m in the car, like it’s happening all over again. At night I wake up from nightmares about being trapped in the car or going over the edge. I’m jumpy with any loud noise, especially traffic sounds, and I avoid certain areas of town altogether. My husband says I’m not myself—more on edge, snapping at little things, exhausted from not sleeping. It’s been like this continuously since the accident.
D012-D018_h004.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D012-D018_h005.question:
It started about a year ago, after I shot that destination wedding where the car crash happened on the way back from the reception. I was in the car behind them and saw everything—the smashed windshield, all the blood, people screaming. I helped until the ambulance came, and I just couldn’t get some of those images out of my head.

Since then, it’s not just that I’m afraid of blood or needles. If I see even a little blood at a wedding—like someone cuts their finger with a boutonniere—I freeze. My body locks up, my heart’s pounding, and I can’t move or lift my camera. Same thing if I’m in a hospital with family; I feel like I’m back at that crash.

I get these vivid nightmares a few times a week where I’m reliving it, and I wake up sweating. During the day, it pops into my head out of nowhere, especially when I’m driving at night or passing that stretch of road. I avoid medical shows, hospitals, even driving certain routes. I’m jumpy with sudden noises at receptions, and my husband says I’m more irritable and on edge. I feel exhausted but sleep is really broken.
D012-D018_h005.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D012-D018_h006.question:
I’ve always been a little squeamish, but this got bad after what happened last year. I was driving home from the salon and came up on a really bad car wreck. There was this guy halfway out of the windshield, bleeding everywhere. I tried to help until the ambulance came, but there was so much blood, and he died right there.

Since then, anything medical sets me off. If I see blood in real life or even on a video, or if someone mentions needles, my chest tightens, my heart races, I start sweating and shaking, and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. I still force myself to go to doctor’s appointments and get blood drawn if I have to, but I’m almost in tears in the chair, gripping the armrest, just trying not to pass out.

It’s not just the blood, though. I keep seeing the accident in my head, especially at night. I have nightmares where I’m back at the scene. I avoid that road completely and hate driving after dark. Loud crashes make me jump and feel like it’s happening again. This has been going on for about a year and it’s really messing with my sleep and my work.
D012-D018_h006.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012-D018_h007.question:
It started about a year ago, after that night we were robbed at gunpoint while closing one of my restaurants. Since then it’s like my whole system is on high alert.

Anything medical sets me off now. If I even see a needle on TV or someone getting blood drawn, my heart jumps into my throat, my hands go numb, and I feel like I’m back on the floor of the office with that guy pointing a gun at me. I nearly passed out when my son scraped his knee—there was just a little blood, but I started shaking and had to leave the room. I avoid hospitals, blood tests, even going with my staff if someone gets hurt in the kitchen. I keep putting off my own checkups because I’m terrified I’ll faint or lose it.

But it’s not just the medical stuff. I have nightmares about the robbery several times a week, wake up sweating, and I can’t stand being in the restaurant late at night. I replay it constantly in my head, jump at loud noises, and I’m exhausted from never really feeling safe anymore.
D012-D018_h007.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012-D018_h008.question:
It started about a year ago, after I was attacked by a big dog on my way back from a client’s house. It knocked me down, tore into my arm and shoulder. Since then, it’s like my whole life has shrunk around this fear.

I can’t be near any dogs now, not even little ones on leashes. Just hearing barking through a window makes my heart race and my legs feel weak. If I even picture a dog in my mind, I start sweating and scanning the room like it’s here. Before I leave for work, I spend a long time planning routes so I won’t pass any houses where I’ve seen dogs. I turned down a good housekeeping job because they had a dog, even though I really need the money.

But it isn’t only the fear. At night I wake up screaming from the same scene, the dog on top of me, its teeth in my arm. I avoid the whole street where it happened. Sudden noises make me jump out of my skin, and I’m always on edge, watching for danger, like something bad is about to happen again.
D012-D018_h008.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012-D018_h009.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after that incident on the night shift. A guy came in with a gun, waving it around, and he fired—missed me by inches but hit a kid behind me. I can still hear the sound and see the blood when I close my eyes.

Since then, I’m jumpy all the time. Loud noises make me duck or grab for my radio. I wake up most nights drenched in sweat from the same nightmare of that hallway. I avoid walking past that part of the building and even try to swap to day shifts, but when I can’t, I just grit my teeth and do it, heart pounding, hands shaking.

I’ve developed this intense fear of dogs too. The guy had this big barking dog outside his car that night, and now just thinking about running into a dog on my patrol sets my chest tight. If I have to pass one—like a coworker’s K9 unit—I force myself, but I’m tense, sweating, and feel like I’m right back in that parking lot. It’s affecting my work and my marriage; my wife says I’m not the same person anymore.
D012-D018_h009.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012-D018_h010.question:
It started about six months ago, after my husband and I got caught in that flash flood when we were driving back from a weekend trip. The car filled with water so fast I really thought we were going to drown. Since then, anything to do with heavy rain or rising water just sets me off.

If it even looks like a storm is coming, my heart starts racing, my chest gets tight, and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. My hands shake so much I can’t even hold my phone properly. I start sweating and feel like I’m right back in the car again. I know it’s just rain, but my body reacts like it’s life-or-death.

I avoid water now as much as I can. I won’t go near lakes or rivers, and I refuse to drive if there’s any chance of a storm. I’ve canceled user interviews and in-person workshops at the office if the forecast looks bad, which is starting to affect my work. I’ll even sleep in the living room to avoid hearing the rain against the bedroom window.
D012-D018_h010.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012-D018_h011.question:
I’ve been running crews on sites for years, so I’m used to loud noises and risky stuff. But ever since what happened two years ago, I’m not the same.

We were pouring concrete when a scaffolding section collapsed. A coworker got crushed right in front of me. There were wasps everywhere because we’d disturbed a nest in the structure. He was screaming, bleeding, and those things were swarming his face. I still see it every night.

Now anything with wasps or bees sets me off. If I hear buzzing, my heart just slams, my hands shake, and I feel like I’m right back there. I can’t go near a job that might have nests unless one of the guys I trust is literally standing next to me; I kind of cling to them and keep scanning around, but I still feel like I’m going to lose it.

I wake up sweating from nightmares about the accident, avoid that part of town, get jumpy with any sudden noise, and I’m always on edge at work. My wife says I’m distant and irritable, but I just feel numb most of the time.
D012-D018_h011.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D012-D018_h012.question:
I work at city hall, so storms are usually just something I check on the weather reports. But since the flood two years ago, when I was trapped in the basement records room as the water came rushing in, thunder and heavy rain feel completely different. 

When a storm rolls in now, I get this surge of panic—heart racing, hands shaking, sweat pouring. I can’t just stay home, so I still go to work and sit through it, but the whole time I’m on edge, staring at the windows, planning escape routes, almost feeling like I’m back down there with the water rising. I don’t show it much, but inside it’s like I’m fighting for my life again.

At night, if there’s thunder, I wake up from these vivid nightmares of drowning. Even without storms, I get sudden images of that day—like flashbacks—just from hearing heavy rain on the roof or seeing flood footage on the news. I avoid the lower levels of the building and parking garages. My wife says I’ve been jumpier, irritable, and I sleep badly most nights, ever since that flood.
D012-D018_h012.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D012-D018_h013.question:
It really started about six months ago, after that car crash on the way back from a tournament. I wasn’t badly injured, but there was a lot of blood—on me, on the other guy—and I honestly thought I was going to die. Since then, everything’s different.

I can’t get the images out of my head. It’s like replaying a horrible clip on loop—random flashbacks during scrims, or suddenly feeling like I’m back in the car when I hear tires screech or even loud popping sounds in-game. I wake up from nightmares drenched in sweat, heart racing, and it’s always the crash or some twisted version of it.

Now anything medical freaks me out. If I see blood—even in a game sometimes—I get dizzy, my heart pounds, I feel like I might pass out. I’ve skipped blood tests and vaccines, and the one time I had to go, I only got through it by having my roommate there, gripping my phone and not looking at anything. I avoid hospitals, driving near that intersection, even talking about the accident. I’m on edge all the time, jumpy, irritable with my team, and I just don’t feel like myself anymore.
D012-D018_h013.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h014.question:
It really started about a year ago, after that car crash on the bridge. A truck hit us from behind and my wife died at the scene. Since then, I can’t stand driving over bridges at all. Even seeing one ahead on the road makes my heart pound, my hands shake, and I feel like I can’t breathe. I start sweating and feel like I’m right back there, hearing the metal crunch and seeing her slumped over.

If my son drives me and I grip the dashboard and keep holding her old scarf, I can just barely get across, but I’m tense the whole time, watching every car, convinced something terrible will happen again. If I’m alone, I’ll go miles out of the way to avoid a bridge altogether.

Nights are the worst. I have nightmares about the accident at least a few times a week and wake up shouting or in tears. During the day I get sudden flashes of it, like a movie in my head, and I jump at loud noises. I don’t sleep well, I’m on edge all the time, and I avoid talking about the crash or driving anywhere that might remind me of it.
D012-D018_h014.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D012-D018_h015.question:
It started about eight months ago, after that car accident on the highway. A truck sideswiped us on a bridge and our car spun toward the edge—thought we were going over. Since then, I can’t handle certain situations at all.

Bridges, tunnels, even parking garages—I freeze up. My heart starts racing, I get sweaty, my hands shake. I picture the car losing control again, like it’s happening right there. I’ll drive twenty minutes out of the way just to avoid an overpass. If I absolutely have to go over one, I only do it if someone’s in the car with me, usually my roommate, and I keep gripping this little pocket knife my dad gave me, like it’s going to protect me or something. If I’m alone, I’ll sometimes just pull over and sit there panicking.

It’s not just the driving. I wake up from nightmares about the crash a few times a week, and at work—selling cars, of all things—I get these flashes of it and zone out. I’m jumpy with loud noises, always on edge, tired from not really sleeping, and I keep replaying the whole thing in my head no matter how much I try not to.
D012-D018_h015.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D012-D018_h016.question:
It started about a year ago after the crash on the highway. I was driving home from a night shift, and a truck slammed into the side of my car. I remember the sound of metal and glass and thinking I was going to die. Since then, I’m terrified of driving, especially on highways and bridges.

Even when I’m just getting ready for work, if I know I have to take that overpass, my chest tightens, my heart races, and I start imagining cars slamming into me. I still force myself to drive because of my job, but the whole time I’m gripping the wheel, sweating, hyper-alert, flinching at every brake light.

It’s not just the driving. I get intrusive images of the crash out of nowhere, especially when I hear sirens at the hospital. I wake up from nightmares, soaked in sweat, feeling like I’m back in the car. I avoid talking about it with coworkers and take back roads even if it adds half an hour. D012-D018_h017.question:

D012-D018_h019.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after that break‑in. I woke up to the sound of glass and a man in our bedroom. He had a knife, and our dog went crazy barking. I honestly thought he was going to kill us. Ever since then, I haven’t been the same.

D012-D018_h020.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after the robbery at my restaurant. The guy had a gun, shoved it in my face, screamed at us, and I honestly thought I was going to die. My chest tightens, my heart races, my hands shake so hard I can’t hold a plate. I feel like I’m going to pass out or throw up.

I can’t be in the restaurant alone anymore. If I have to lock up, my husband or one of the chefs has to stay with me. Just knowing someone is there is the only way I can get through it. If the alarm beeps too loud or the music cuts off suddenly, I lose it.

D012-D018_h021.question:

While we were live, a truck jackknifed right in front of us. I watched a car get crushed; I honestly thought I was going to die. Since then, I haven’t been the same.

I can’t just not go—I still have to get to the studio—so I white‑knuckle it, sometimes pulling over to breathe, but I push through because I don’t have a choice. D012-D018_h022.question:

D012-D018_h023.question:
